listeningDraft.importTranscript: You hear part of a presentation about the early  history of  salt. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. In my presentation, I'm going to talk about salt. In modern times, when we talk about salt, people may associate it with high blood pressure or increased heart risk. and many health experts warn that we should use less salt in our meals and dishes. However, we should not ignore its importance in our cuisine. and even in early human history, salt is one of the oldest, most ubiquitous  food seasonings. The taste of salt is one of the basic human tastes. More importantly, salt plays an indispensable role in the health of human beings. For example, it regulates the body’s acid base balance. Because of its importance to survival, salt has often been considered a valuable commodity during human history. This can be tracked all the way back to ancient Greece, ancient Egypt and ancient Rome, when salt was highly valued and used as a method of trade and currency. In ancient Rome, the busiest road leading to the city was the Via Solaria, which means the salt route. In English, a soldier’s pay, which partly consisted of salt, was known as solarium Argentum in Latin, from which we derived the English word salary. a soldier’s salary was cut if he was "not worth his salt", an expression still used today. In fact, salt was not only the first condiment discovered, but also the first preservative. We know today that food goes bad because microorganisms in the food multiply in abundance and a high salt environment is not conducive to microbial reproduction. extremely high concentrations of salt can even kill microorganisms in the food. The ancients certainly didn’t know this, but they did know that salted food can be preserved for a long time. The use of salt as a preservative can be traced to ancient Sweden. At first, hunting was the principal means of livelihood. In this case, meat supplies were unlikely to be frequent. What's more, fewer animals were available for hunting. In order to ensure the supply of meat, many families in Sweden began to raise animals in the surrounding forests during the summer when the weather was suitable for animals to survive. These animals were fed every day until about three to four months later . That's in October they were ready to be butchered for meat. and That was the only month when ancient Swedish people had fresh meat on their table. Then, with the continuous increase in productivity, people finally had some meat left. however, how to store the meat had become a headache until someone invented a whole new way to preserve food salting. people tried to keep meat from going bad by adding some salt to it and it could be preserved for several months and even years. There was evidence that salt was widely used to preserve meat. Historical documents in 1573 recorded the Swedish king’s everyday meals, mentioning that 175$ of meat was consumed each year, but over $150 was salty. From this we can clearly see the importance of salt in Sweden at that time. In addition, the documents also noted that the annual sales of beer in Sweden soared during that period and this must be related to high levels of salt in their food. Now let’s turn to the sources of salt. Where is salt from? Well, salt is common in nature. It has long been found that salts can be extracted from seawater mineral deposits, saline lakes, brine, spring, etc. among which the two most important ones are oceans and basins. on the floor of the latter often lie deserts where traces of salt can be found, such as the sahara. Furthermore, the quality of different  salt types varies a lot. For example, salt from seawater is always mixed with impurities, so after the salt is dried, the sediments and other chemicals need to be purified before eating. However, this is not the case. with salt from spring water we can hardly find any impurities and the salt level is much more concentrated. Then how did people distribute salt around the world? Of course, in modern times we have various ways of transporting goods, but in ancient times it was not the case. take ancient Sweden we mentioned before as an example. Because of a heavy use of salt in the diet, Sweden could not feed itself and had to import large amounts of salt from other countries in order to make sure they could buy enough salt from abroad. The Swedish had to attach great importance to shipping and keep it undamaged, as it was the most crucial way at that time. while in other ancient countries, in order to distribute salt to other places, groups of men were employed. They put bags of salt on their shoulders or backs and moved them to the surrounding regions. and gradually these people were considered as a mode of transport in early times. Later, with the improvement of traffic conditions, salt trade between different regions was boosted and long distance  food trade was also promoted, making communication between different cultures more frequent. and that is the end of part four

speakingTests.transcript:
[Part 1] Q: What is the most challenging part of your work or studies?
A: Actually, the most challenge part of my studies is when I face the Meetum test or the intern test Those are when I have to fully focus on my studies and Also manage my time appropriately and also Um, try anything to reduce stress.

[Part 1] Q: Has your hometown changed much since you were a child?
A: Actually, yes, my hotel used to be remote area, which is just small houses, trees, and forests. But when I visited it recently, I found out that there appear buildings, offices, and many facilities and infrastructures.

[Part 1 follow-up] Q: What do you think about these changes?
A: I think these changes are good for my hometown because it can promote the like it can push the development of my hometown and like increase the standard of living for their residents.

[Part 1] Q: What kind of food do you enjoy eating the most?
A: To be honest, I enjoy eating the Vietnamese traditional food most because I find it very delicious with the like, any dish which is mixed with the fish sauce and cooked by the Vietnamese chef is very tasty to me.

[Part 1] Q: Is there a hobby you would like to try in the future? Why?
A: I think it could be the playing golf, I have seen that I saw my father playing golf when I was young and I find that this sport is interesting and if I have a chance in the future I would try it.

[Part 1] Q: Do you usually get enough sleep? How does sleep affect your mood?
A: Actually, I do get enough sleep and however, every time I am not sleeping enough, I will be very tired and I can focus on my work.

[Part 2] Q: Describe an important decision you have made.
A: I want to say that registering a camp to Germany is a very important decision that I have made recently. I did it when I was in Hanoi, when I went to a German center called Citizen and they introduced me this camp program and they told me that this program can change how I think about my future, my university and how the society and residents in the Europe work and yes I find it very interesting and I think that this decision is very vital to me because I can develop various skills when I was in the camp and also I have made many friends from various countries like Russian or Norway and I find the experience is very, very horrible to me.

[Part 2 follow-up] Q: Has your opinion about this changed over time?
A: I have a question. What is the term this in your question mean?

[Part 3] Q: Why do some people find it hard to make important decisions?
A: from my perspective, this is because they are scared about the outcome that they can face when they make any important decisions like in Vietnam, some students scared of choosing their future university because they are afraid that they cannot find their dream jobs when they choose that university.

[Part 3 follow-up] Q: Can you think of any ways to overcome this fear of the outcome?
A: I think the best way for me to overcome this fear is I always have a specific plan about my future, my action, and my dream, like I will have the plan for my day, my week, my month, and my years belong to the goals I want to achieve in that day, week, month, or year. This specific plan can help me see everything clearly and overcome the fear of the outcome.

[Part 3] Q: Should young people make their own career choices, or follow their parents' advice?
A: I think people shouldn't make their own career choices this is because only they know what exactly they want and what exactly their talents can be applied and their parents advice can be useful sometimes but in some cases it can enhance their dreams.

[Part 3 follow-up] Q: How can parents' advice enhance their children's dreams?
A: I think parents are the people who have experienced many years and they know what is suitable for their children. What is worth for their children? So in some cases their advice can accelerate their children's dreams because the children can avoid making wrong decisions. Like their parents did in the past.

[Part 3] Q: Is it better to take time to decide, or to act quickly?
A: In my opinion, it is better to take time to decide rather than to act quickly. This is because when you sit down and think about a problem, before deciding, you can sit clearly and you can avoid any emotion to affect you in deciding what to do, instead of act quickly without seeing the negative outcome or trade off.

[Part 3 follow-up] Q: Can you give an example of a time when acting quickly led to a negative outcome?
A: Yes, actually acting quickly can lead to negative outcome when the emotion affects you to ignore the outcome or the trade off you have to make. The famous example are the crime criminals when they act everything quickly without seeing the negative consequences.

[Part 3] Q: How do cultural values shape the decisions people make?
A: I think, yes, cultural values of a person is what he observed throughout some early years of his life and in some cases it can be deeply injected to his subconscious mind. And it can, but like it just can affect when a person acts very quickly without seeing the outcome. However, when a person sits down, sees the outcome and makes clear decisions with calculated trade-off the cultural values.

markingExamples.text:
IELTS Writing Bank
Structural Blueprint Edition (v3)
Batch 1 + Batch 2 — 16 entries
Crawl date: 2026-06-11
Cấu trúc mỗi entry
Đề bài → Essay Blueprint (sentence-by-sentence) → Cụm tiêu biểu → Key Vocabulary → Band Features → Examiner Commentary → Common Pitfalls
Schema v3 không tái tạo essay gốc. Học bằng cách hiểu CẤU TRÚC, KỸ THUẬT và VOCAB - sau đó tự viết lại.
Source: https://howtodoielts.com — Dave (ex-IELTS examiner)
Use: Personal study only

Mục lục
Task 1 Academic (10 entries)
T1-001  Bamboo Fabric (Cambridge 20)  [process_diagram]
T1-002  Public Library, Little Chalfont (Cambridge 20)  [mixed_charts]

Cover cả 3 tables. Số liệu đầy đủ với cả con số tuyệt đối và % (60,515 or 76%). Overview chỉ ra xu hướng dài hạn.
Coherence & Cohesion
Tham chiếu ngược ('pattern detailed above only increased in velocity') để kết nối đoạn 2-3. 'In contrast' để đối lập trong cùng đoạn.
Lexical Resource
Vocab thay đổi tỷ trọng đa dạng (surged, slipped, widened, increased in velocity). Quantifier đa dạng.
Grammatical Range & Accuracy
'there occurred a pronounced shift' - inversion structure. Mix simple past + past perfect.
🧑‍🏫 Examiner Commentary (Bình luận)
Tables theo thời gian là dạng dễ viết khô khan. Bài này hay ở chỗ tổ chức theo 3 mốc thời gian (1800, 1900, 2000) thay vì theo từng quận - tránh lặp 'Manhattan...' 5 lần. Học viên nên xác định trục tổ chức TRƯỚC khi viết: theo thời gian, theo nhóm, hay theo size.
⚠️ Common Pitfalls (Lỗi thường gặp)
Liệt kê thẳng từng quận một (Manhattan ... Brooklyn ... Bronx...) → bài thành table 2 lần
Không kết hợp số tuyệt đối + % → mất tính phân tích
Dùng đi dùng lại 'increased' / 'decreased' thay vì verb mạnh (surged, slipped, plummeted, soared)

markingExamples.text:
IELTS Task 2 Error Correction Report (Full Version)
Essay Topic
Ecotourism in remote destinations and indigenous communities is becoming increasingly popular. Is it a positive or negative development for the local inhabitants and the natural environment?
Original
Ecotourism in rural regions and local communities in becoming more and more popular. While it can lead to some drawbacks, I firmly believe that the overall benefits far outweigh the negatives.
On the one hand, some individuals think that ecotourism, despite alleviating the trash wasted into the environment compared to other type of tourism, can still affect the local residents' lifestyle. Therefore, it can lead to the erosion of conventional practices and values, as the locals have to adapt in order to cater to tourists' expectation. To be more precise, a remote area, if chosen as a tourist attraction, will face several issues such as noise pollution (because more people means more noise) or light pollution (more buildings and facilities will be constructed to face the travellers' demands). Overall, by indicating the disadvantages of tourism, the opinion considers that tourism is not a positive development.
On the other hand, indigenous people can receive more benefits than which they have to pay. From some perspective, ecotourism is one of the best way a rural community can have not only to conserve their culture, but also raise their general income, which promote the area's economy. Tourism can also advertise the destination to the world. For example, in the far north and northwest of the North Vietnam, where bordering China and Laos, existing a number of ethnic groups of people living in villages on the mountainside, separated from the open world. In that situation, ecotourism is almost the most effective way to not only connect the regions to the other parts of the country, but also create more opportunities for their people in occupation and trading.
In conclusion, I believe that the benefits ,which ecotourism brings to the indigenous regions, can outweigh the drawbacks to become positive development.

1. Full Error Correction (Original => Revised)
Introduction
Ecotourism in rural regions and local communities in becoming more and more popular. => Ecotourism in rural regions and local communities is becoming increasingly popular.
Note: “in becoming” is incorrect verb form. Use “is becoming”. “Increasingly” is more formal than “more and more”.

While it can lead to some drawbacks, I firmly believe that the overall benefits far outweigh the negatives. => (Correct – no change needed)

Body Paragraph 1
On the one hand, some individuals think that ecotourism, despite alleviating the trash wasted into the environment compared to other type of tourism, can still affect the local residents’ lifestyle. => On the one hand, some individuals argue that ecotourism, despite reducing waste released into the environment compared to other types of tourism, can still affect the lifestyle of local residents.
Note:
“the trash wasted” ❌ → “waste released” ✔ (natural collocation)
“other type” ❌ → “other types” ✔ (plural)

Therefore, it can lead to the erosion of conventional practices and values, as the locals have to adapt in order to cater to tourists’ expectation. => Therefore, it can lead to the erosion of traditional practices and values, as locals have to adapt in order to meet tourists’ expectations.

To be more precise, a remote area, if chosen as a tourist attraction, will face several issues such as noise pollution (because more people means more noise) or light pollution (more buildings and facilities will be constructed to face the travellers’ demands). => To be more precise, a remote area, if chosen as a tourist attraction, may face several issues such as noise pollution (as more visitors generate more noise) and light pollution (as more buildings and facilities are constructed to meet travellers’ demands).

Overall, by indicating the disadvantages of tourism, the opinion considers that tourism is not a positive development. => Overall, this perspective suggests that tourism is not a positive development.

Body Paragraph 2
On the other hand, indigenous people can receive more benefits than which they have to pay. => On the other hand, indigenous people can gain more benefits than the costs they incur.

From some perspective, ecotourism is one of the best way a rural community can have not only to conserve their culture, but also raise their general income, which promote the area’s economy. => From some perspectives, ecotourism is one of the best ways a rural community can not only conserve its culture but also increase its income, which promotes the local economy.

Tourism can also advertise the destination to the world. => Tourism can also promote the destination to the world.

For example, in the far north and northwest of the North Vietnam, where bordering China and Laos, existing a number of ethnic groups of people living in villages on the mountainside, separated from the open world. => For example, in the far north and northwest of Vietnam, which border China and Laos, there are a number of ethnic groups living in mountainous villages, relatively isolated from the outside world.

In that situation, ecotourism is almost the most effective way to not only connect the regions to the other parts of the country, but also create more opportunities for their people in occupation and trading. => In this context, ecotourism is one of the most effective ways to not only connect these regions to other parts of the country but also create more opportunities for local people in employment and trade.

Conclusion
In conclusion, I believe that the benefits ,which ecotourism brings to the indigenous regions, can outweigh the drawbacks to become positive development. => In conclusion, I believe that the benefits that ecotourism brings to indigenous regions outweigh the drawbacks, making it a positive development.

2. Minimal-Edit Full Essay (Clean Version)
Ecotourism in rural regions and local communities is becoming increasingly popular. While it can lead to some drawbacks, I firmly believe that the overall benefits far outweigh the negatives.
On the one hand, some individuals argue that ecotourism, despite reducing waste released into the environment compared to other types of tourism, can still affect the lifestyle of local residents. Therefore, it can lead to the erosion of traditional practices and values, as locals have to adapt in order to meet tourists’ expectations. To be more precise, a remote area, if chosen as a tourist attraction, may face several issues such as noise pollution and light pollution, as more buildings and facilities are constructed to meet travellers’ demands. Overall, this perspective suggests that tourism is not a positive development.
On the other hand, indigenous people can gain more benefits than the costs they incur. From some perspectives, ecotourism is one of the best ways a rural community can not only conserve its culture but also increase its income, which promotes the local economy. Tourism can also promote the destination to the world. For example, in the far north and northwest of Vietnam, which border China and Laos, there are a number of ethnic groups living in mountainous villages, relatively isolated from the outside world. In this context, ecotourism is one of the most effective ways to connect these regions to other parts of the country and create more opportunities for local people in employment and trade.
In conclusion, I believe that the benefits that ecotourism brings to indigenous regions outweigh the drawbacks, making it a positive development.

3. Logic & Organization Map
Thesis (Clear Version)
Ecotourism has some disadvantages, but it is overall a positive development for local communities.
Paragraph Breakdown
Body 1
Topic: Disadvantages
Claims: cultural erosion, pollution
Gap: lacks deeper explanation (HOW culture changes)
Body 2
Topic: Advantages
Claims: income, cultural preservation, connection
Gap: example not deeply explained

Improved Band 7+ Outline
Introduction
Paraphrase topic
Clear opinion
Body 1
Cultural disruption
Environmental pressure
Explain HOW it happens
Body 2
Economic benefits
Cultural preservation
Specific example
Conclusion
Restate opinion

Fix these: 1. ___ environment is important. 2. ___ tourists affect ___ culture. 3. This is one of ___ best ways.

test.transcript: You hear part of a presentation about the early  history of  salt. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. In my presentation, I'm going to talk about salt. In modern times, when we talk about salt, people may associate it with high blood pressure or increased heart risk. and many health experts warn that we should use less salt in our meals and dishes. However, we should not ignore its importance in our cuisine. and even in early human history, salt is one of the oldest, most ubiquitous  food seasonings. The taste of salt is one of the basic human tastes. More importantly, salt plays an indispensable role in the health of human beings. For example, it regulates the body’s acid base balance. Because of its importance to survival, salt has often been considered a valuable commodity during human history. This can be tracked all the way back to ancient Greece, ancient Egypt and ancient Rome, when salt was highly valued and used as a method of trade and currency. In ancient Rome, the busiest road leading to the city was the Via Solaria, which means the salt route. In English, a soldier’s pay, which partly consisted of salt, was known as solarium Argentum in Latin, from which we derived the English word salary. a soldier’s salary was cut if he was "not worth his salt", an expression still used today. In fact, salt was not only the first condiment discovered, but also the first preservative. We know today that food goes bad because microorganisms in the food multiply in abundance and a high salt environment is not conducive to microbial reproduction. extremely high concentrations of salt can even kill microorganisms in the food. The ancients certainly didn’t know this, but they did know that salted food can be preserved for a long time. The use of salt as a preservative can be traced to ancient Sweden. At first, hunting was the principal means of livelihood. In this case, meat supplies were unlikely to be frequent. What's more, fewer animals were available for hunting. In order to ensure the supply of meat, many families in Sweden began to raise animals in the surrounding forests during the summer when the weather was suitable for animals to survive. These animals were fed every day until about three to four months later . That's in October they were ready to be butchered for meat. and That was the only month when ancient Swedish people had fresh meat on their table. Then, with the continuous increase in productivity, people finally had some meat left. however, how to store the meat had become a headache until someone invented a whole new way to preserve food salting. people tried to keep meat from going bad by adding some salt to it and it could be preserved for several months and even years. There was evidence that salt was widely used to preserve meat. Historical documents in 1573 recorded the Swedish king’s everyday meals, mentioning that 175$ of meat was consumed each year, but over $150 was salty. From this we can clearly see the importance of salt in Sweden at that time. In addition, the documents also noted that the annual sales of beer in Sweden soared during that period and this must be related to high levels of salt in their food. Now let’s turn to the sources of salt. Where is salt from? Well, salt is common in nature. It has long been found that salts can be extracted from seawater mineral deposits, saline lakes, brine, spring, etc. among which the two most important ones are oceans and basins. on the floor of the latter often lie deserts where traces of salt can be found, such as the sahara. Furthermore, the quality of different  salt types varies a lot. For example, salt from seawater is always mixed with impurities, so after the salt is dried, the sediments and other chemicals need to be purified before eating. However, this is not the case. with salt from spring water we can hardly find any impurities and the salt level is much more concentrated. Then how did people distribute salt around the world? Of course, in modern times we have various ways of transporting goods, but in ancient times it was not the case. take ancient Sweden we mentioned before as an example. Because of a heavy use of salt in the diet, Sweden could not feed itself and had to import large amounts of salt from other countries in order to make sure they could buy enough salt from abroad. The Swedish had to attach great importance to shipping and keep it undamaged, as it was the most crucial way at that time. while in other ancient countries, in order to distribute salt to other places, groups of men were employed. They put bags of salt on their shoulders or backs and moved them to the surrounding regions. and gradually these people were considered as a mode of transport in early times. Later, with the improvement of traffic conditions, salt trade between different regions was boosted and long distance  food trade was also promoted, making communication between different cultures more frequent. and that is the end of part four
